prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage
for the development of ligand-controlled palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: I have changed my second part from nanopore sensing (B050) to Pd-catalysed C-N coupling (B030) and keep base editing (B058) as the first. B058 has the broadest support in the room (five of eight members include it, always with Liu alone), and its chemical content is the evolved deaminase: a TadA variant that acts on DNA, which no natural enzyme does, and control of editing window and product outcome, coupled to a programmable binder so that one base is converted without a double-strand break. That is designed reactivity, not only a delivery of CRISPR biology, and it has reached patients. B030 is the best-defined case on the list on the points I pressed in round 1: what was discovered, by whom and when. The new principle is a family of bulky, electron-rich ligands that make oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination work for a very wide range of free amines with a base, supported by mechanistic work and more than 25 years of independent use. Kosugi's aminostannane coupling needed stoichiometric tin reagents and is a precedent, not a co-discovery. Two named laureates for B030 and one for B058 give three people in total. I do not claim the two parts form one story. Each stands alone, one is a mature method that changed how bonds are made in flasks and factories, the other a young tool that rewrites a base in a genome, and the citations can be explained separately to a broad audience.
statement.case_against: Pairing unrelated achievements risks looking like a trade, which several members, myself included, said in round 1. B058 follows the 2020 CRISPR prize closely, its clinical record is short, and a Liu-only citation leaves out Komor and Gaudelli, who ran the decisive first experiments, and Kondo and Nishida, whose Target-AID work was independent and close in time. B030 can be read as the same palladium chemistry as the 2010 cross-coupling prize with a different heteroatom, and I cannot fully settle that question as a physicist; I rely on the synthetic chemists for it. I also gave up B050 partly because I favoured it for physical reasons, and a reviewer might say I am now following the vote count. I am not: the reasons are attribution and what was shown, not support numbers. If B058 is judged too soon after CRISPR, B030 alone would be a defensible but narrower prize.

responses.point: Zou ranks B030 first, separates Kosugi's stoichiometric tin-amide precedent from the free-amine, ligand-controlled catalytic cycle of Buchwald and Hartwig, and asks the committee to test the priority record and Migita-type precedents before settling.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 question to Somfai about what is new in kind. The change from stoichiometric tin amides to a general catalytic cycle with free amines, driven by a ligand design principle, is a different discovery and not only more scope. I agree the priority record should be checked and that Kosugi is named in the citation context but not as a laureate. Your criticism of my nanopore part also moved me: I cannot fix the attribution among Bayley, Akeson, Deamer, Branton and Kasianowicz within three names, and Branton may no longer be living. I have therefore adopted your B030 and B058 pairing, with B050 as an alternative.

responses.point: Somfai argues that B030 rests on mechanistic work on oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination, not only on scope, and that evolved deaminase chemistry answers the question of what base editing adds beyond CRISPR.
responses.response: The mechanistic evidence is what a physicist wants to see, a clear principle with quantitative support, and it separates the method from a ligand screen. I accept it as the reason B030 is more than an extension of the 2010 prize, although I recognise some colleagues may still weigh it as a follow-on, and I defer to you and Zou on the synthetic details. We agree the citation for B058 should say nucleobase conversion by an engineered enzyme, so that it is not read as a genome-cutting tool.

responses.point: Aqvist argues that base editing is a chemist's invention and a different mechanism from CRISPR cleavage, and that a Liu-only attribution is defensible, treating Target-AID as a citation caveat.
responses.response: I agree with the Liu-alone attribution and with reading the 2020 prize as recognising a tool that cuts DNA, whereas base editing needs no break. Naming Liu alone keeps the whole configuration at three people with room for a second part. I differ with you on weight only slightly: I still think the Kondo and Nishida dates should be examined, and the citation should not claim more than first conversion of a base by a deaminase fused to a Cas nickase, so that their independent work is not contradicted.

responses.point: Chabes ranks targeted protein degradation first as a designable chemical reaction, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and admits that no degrader is approved and that Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim have serious claims.
responses.response: The induced-proximity principle is strong and I keep B008 as an alternative. I still do not put it in the preferred configuration because the credit among at least eight names does not reduce to three without arbitrary choices, and PROTACs and molecular glues read as two stories, as you and Somfai both note. If an approved degrader appears, I would reconsider and would then want the citation to define one strand, not a composite.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a two-part prize of unrelated achievements, or prefers B058 alone or a single coherent topic.
Whether B030 is seen as new in kind relative to the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and whether the priority record fully supports Buchwald and Hartwig over Kosugi and Migita-type precedents.
Whether naming Liu alone is acceptable given Komor and Gaudelli, and how Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID work should be acknowledged.
Whether the 2020 CRISPR prize makes base editing too close a follow-on, and whether its clinical record is long enough.
Whether B050 could be settled on attribution if the status of Branton and the roles of Deamer and Kasianowicz were clarified.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to any shortlisted candidate. My research on nanostructures and molecular motors is close in spirit to nanopore physics (B050), which I no longer include in my preferred configuration, and I am a Lund colleague of Somfai and Sparr, with no collaboration with either on a candidate. I defer to the synthetic chemists on B030 and to the biochemists on B058 details.
